text: Chapter 3 assumed lineage was already traced and available to walk — upstream for root cause analysis, downstream for impact analysis. Lineage documentation is what makes that walk possible in the first place: the recorded, shareable version of the dependency graph, instead of something that lives only in one engineer's memory. Good documentation answers three questions for every dependency: what's connected, what direction connects them, and who's responsible for each side.

Nodes are the datasets, fields, reports, and systems themselves — each needs a stable name and ideally a short description, the kind covered in Metadata Management's glossary and data dictionary chapters. Edges are the dependency itself: which node feeds which, and critically, the transformation and business rule from Lesson 13 that happens at that hop, not just the fact a connection exists. Ownership is who maintains each node, so impact analysis or root cause analysis finds a person to contact, not a dead end.

A wiki page or shared doc is easy to write and flexible, but goes stale fast — nobody updates it on every pipeline change. A metadata repository or data catalog is centralized and searchable, tied to the glossary and dictionary, but only as good as what's actually entered into it. A dedicated lineage tool can auto-generate and stay current, covered next lesson, though it requires tooling investment and may miss undocumented manual steps. Most organizations end up using more than one of these at once.

Lesson 13 made the case that an arrow alone — StagingView feeds FactTable — is only half the picture. Lineage documentation has to capture both halves: the structural graph, which this lesson focuses on, and the transformation logic behind each edge, which a diagram or linked description usually carries. Documentation missing ownership tells you what's affected by a change but not who to tell — defeating half the point of Lesson 15's change impact assessment. One half alone is incomplete.

Next lesson: lineage diagrams — the visual format most people actually picture when they hear lineage documentation, the conventions that keep boxes and arrows readable instead of a tangle, and how to match the level of detail in a diagram to whoever's actually going to read it.
